title: A whole surah opens on a short scale.
subtitle: Why small cheating gets a loud warning
then: The traders of Makkah lived by the scale and the measuring cup. Ibn Kathir reports that when the Prophet ﷺ reached Madinah, people there were known for cheating on measure. {idea}This surah was recited, and they began to give full measure.{/idea}
now: The invoice rounded up by fifteen minutes. The used phone sold with the cracked corner hidden in the photos. The extra item you let slide at the self-checkout. {trap}Small enough that nobody checks.{/trap}
old: A little off the top is just how business works.
new: The small cut is exactly what Allah chose to open a surah with.
try: Check one bill, timesheet or sale you made this week. Make sure the other person got their full due.

title: When they receive, they want every last grain.
subtitle: The first half of a double standard

row.title: I just want what is fair

then: Ibn Kathir explains that these people took their right in full and pressed for extra when buying from others. {trap}They knew exactly what a full measure looked like{/trap}, because they insisted on it for themselves.
now: You count the change from the cashier twice. You chase the refund to the last cent. You notice the moment a colleague takes credit for your idea. {idea}You already know what fairness feels like from the receiving end.{/idea}
old: Making sure I get my full share is just being careful.
new: How I measure for myself shows that I know the standard I owe others.
try: Notice one place today where you insist on your full share. Ask if you give the same to others.

title: When they give, the scale quietly shrinks.
subtitle: The second half of the double standard

row.title: two measures
sub: one for me, one for you

then: Measuring by volume or weighing by scale, they made others lose. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah commands full weight elsewhere, and that {trap}the people of Shu'ayb were destroyed for this same cheating{/trap}.
now: You want your manager to pay overtime to the minute, but your own lunch break stretches. You want the landlord to fix things fast, but your rent is late. {idea}Two rulers in one pocket.{/idea}
old: Everyone shaves a bit off when they are the one paying.
new: Giving less than I would accept is the very thing this verse names.
try: Give one person today a little more than their due: time, effort or money.

title: Cheating starts where the thought of rising again stops.
subtitle: The root behind the short scale
then: The surah introduction explains that this one evil is given as an example of what happens when people forget the Hereafter. {idea}Honesty that rests only on being watched breaks when no one is watching.{/idea} The verse asks: do they not even think about it?
now: Working from home with no one checking your screen. The expense form nobody audits. The exam where the invigilator steps out. {trap}The test is not the rule. It is who you think is looking.{/trap}
old: If no one will ever find out, it does not really count.
new: Someone will raise me and ask, and that changes the private moments.
try: In one unwatched moment today, do the honest thing and remind yourself why.

title: Small profit, set against a tremendous Day.
subtitle: Putting the gain on the right scale
then: Ibn Kathir describes the Day as one of great horror and tremendous fright, before the One who knows hidden secrets. {idea}The verse makes the cheater's small gain look its real size.{/idea}
now: You lie awake over a fifty-dollar dispute with a seller. The anger at a colleague over a parking spot. {reward}Put it next to the Great Day and most of it shrinks.{/reward}
old: This little advantage is worth fighting for.
new: Next to the Great Day, what I am grabbing is almost nothing.
try: Pick one petty gain you are chasing and let it go today.

title: Everyone stands, and the Lord of all is before them.
subtitle: The standing that ends every deal
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that people will stand until some sink in sweat to the middle of their ears, each according to their deeds. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge from the hardship of that standing{/idea} in his night prayer.
now: You stand in a long queue at the bank and feel your patience thin. You wait in a hospital corridor for news. {reward}Standing makes you honest about what you have and have not done.{/reward}
old: I answer to my boss, my clients, maybe the tax office.
new: In the end I stand before the Lord of everything, and so does everyone I dealt with.
try: In your next prayer, ask Allah to make the standing easy for you, as the Prophet ﷺ did.

title: No. The record of the wicked is kept in Sijjin.
subtitle: Where a cheating life is filed
then: The verse opens with a sharp No, cutting off the idea that no reckoning comes. Ibn Kathir says Sijjin is taken from the word for prison and means {trap}straitened, narrow circumstances{/trap}, the final abode of the wicked.
now: Every app keeps a history: your search log, your messages, your bank statements. {idea}You already live in a world where nothing is truly deleted.{/idea} The verse says your deeds have a record too.
old: Once it is done and forgotten, it is gone.
new: What I do is filed somewhere, and the file has a destination.
try: Tonight, think of one thing you would not want in your record. Ask Allah's forgiveness for it.

title: And what will make you know what Sijjin is?
subtitle: A question that makes it heavier
then: Ibn Kathir says this question expresses how great the matter is: {trap}an eternal prison and a painful torment{/trap}. The listeners in Makkah were stopped mid-sentence and made to wonder.
now: A doctor says, "Sit down, we need to talk." You know before the words come that it is serious. {idea}The question works the same way. It makes you sit down.{/idea}
old: I already know roughly what the warnings say.
new: Allah's question tells me this is bigger than I have pictured.
try: When you hear a warning in the Quran today, stop for one breath before moving on.

title: A register inscribed. Nothing added, nothing erased.
subtitle: The record is closed and complete
then: Ibn Kathir, citing Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi, explains that the destination is {trap}inscribed, written, and completed. No one can add to it and no one can remove from it.{/trap}
now: The email you cannot unsend. The exam paper already handed in. The contract signed and filed. {reward}Right now your page is still open, and repentance still writes on it.{/reward}
old: There will always be time to fix my record.
new: One day the register closes. Today it is still open.
try: Do one thing today you would want written in your record: a call, a charity, an apology.

title: Woe that Day to those who called it a lie.
subtitle: The second woe of the surah
then: The surah began with woe to those who cheat. Now it ties a second woe to those who deny. Ibn Kathir says woe means {trap}destruction and devastation{/trap} when they come to their imprisonment.
now: You may never say "I deny the Day" out loud. But the way you split a bill or fill a timesheet speaks too. {idea}Denial can live in habits, not only in words.{/idea}
old: I believe in the Day, so this warning is not about me.
new: My daily dealings show how much I really believe the Day is coming.
try: Pick one habit that acts as if no Day is coming. Change it a little today.

title: They deny the Day when everything is repaid.
subtitle: What exactly they refused to believe
then: Ibn Kathir explains that they did not believe the Day would happen and {trap}considered it far-fetched{/trap}. In early Makkah, surah after surah was revealed to set this belief in people's hearts.
now: Someone wrongs you and gets away with it. A kindness you did goes unthanked for years. {reward}The Day of Recompense means neither is lost.{/reward}
old: Some things in life just never get settled.
new: There is a Day set aside to repay everything, the good I did included.
try: Think of one unthanked good deed you did. Leave its reward with Allah and feel lighter.

title: Only the one who keeps crossing lines denies it.
subtitle: Denial and wrongdoing feed each other

row.title: conduct shapes belief
sub: what I do bends what I accept

then: Ibn Kathir describes this person as {trap}transgressive in deeds and sinful in speech{/trap}: he lies when he speaks, breaks promises, and is abusive when he argues. Denying the Day lets him carry on.
now: Once you have padded one expense claim, the next is easier, and the rules start to feel silly. {idea}Behaviour quietly writes your beliefs for you.{/idea} Keeping small promises keeps the heart honest.
old: My doubts come from thinking, not from how I live.
new: The lines I keep crossing can make the truth harder for me to accept.
try: Keep one small promise today exactly as you made it.
